title: Expand the labeled corpus to the n the power analysis derives
description:
Serves STRATEGY risk 1. Blocks IDF weighting, threshold fitting, and calibration — all three overfit at current size.

All three corpora together hold 54 outcomes and 85 expected labels. Distinguishing a 0.15 miss rate from 0.30 at 80% power needs labels on the order of hundreds, not tens. Until then every fitted parameter is fitted to noise, and every corpus is spent the moment it is measured against twice.

Authorship discipline matters more than volume: outcomes must be authored by someone who has not read the keyword catalog, or the expansion recreates the circularity construct-gsf named. Held-out and fresh both died of exactly this.
acceptance_criteria: Corpus reaches the label count derived in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 1; authorship provenance recorded per outcome; a documented split discipline that keeps a genuine held-out partition unspent.
notes:
2026-08-04 LANDED. 144 outcomes, eight settings, eight authoring agents each forbidden to read any file in this repository; two independent coders over all 144 seeing only the ten domain names and their concerns; 17 disagreements adjudicated with both raw label sets kept per outcome.

Split deterministically by position inside each setting, so both halves carry all eight settings and neither is one author's whole output:
  tests/kernel/implication/fixtures/unspent-outcomes.json  72 outcomes / 83 labels — MEASURED
  tests/kernel/implication/fixtures/sealed-outcomes.json   72 outcomes / 84 labels — SEALED

Both halves clear the 64 labels RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 1 derives for distinguishing 0.30 from 0.15 at 80% power. The seal is a test, not an intention: tests/kernel/implication/corpus-split.test.ts fails if any string literal in src/, scripts/ or tests/ names the sealed file, and the split test itself may not import the matcher.

MEASURED ON LANDING (measured half): miss 0.663 (55/83, Wilson [0.556, 0.755]), over 0.404 (19/47), silent 33/72. Inter-coder Krippendorff alpha MASI 0.9270 on that half, 0.8955 across all 144.

CAVEAT ON RECORD, in the fixtures and in the document: authors, coders and adjudicator are all models of one family, so observed agreement is an upper bound on independent agreement. Blindness buys independence of WORDING, not of error — and wording is what the earlier corpora leaked. Stage 2 (construct-3ft) is still the measurement that settles the annotation floor.

Follow-ups filed at discovery: construct-13n (escalate-on-silence reaches 38 of 55 misses here vs 1 of 6 on the older corpora). construct-4jq updated with the measurement it asked for and stays open.
close_reason: Corpus built, split, sealed and measured: 144 blind-authored outcomes, double-coded (alpha MASI 0.9270 on the measured half), 83 labels measured and 84 sealed, both halves above the 64 the power analysis derives. Provenance per outcome, split discipline enforced by tests/kernel/implication/corpus-split.test.ts. Full gate green.

title: Multi-coder agreement study: establish whether 0.15 is a goal or a fiction
description:
Serves STRATEGY risk 1 and Phase 2 exit. Blocks all further catalog tuning.

Every corpus has one author, which construct-gsf identified as circular. The unexamined consequence is that nobody knows how much of the residual miss rate is model error and how much is label disagreement. If two careful people disagree about whether 'run a raffle for anyone who joins before Friday' implicates marketing-claims, no classifier can be scored below that disagreement rate, and a target set beneath it is unreachable by construction.

Have 2-3 people independently label the same 30 outcomes against the catalog, with no discussion. Compute Krippendorff's alpha (handles multi-label and missing labels, which Cohen's kappa does not) and derive the Bayes error floor the observed alpha implies. Cost is hours; it determines whether a program goal is real.

Needs Gerald: requires recruiting labelers.
acceptance_criteria: Reported in two stages, and the stages are not interchangeable. STAGE 1 (model coders, satisfiable without a human): Krippendorff's alpha over >=30 outcomes and >=2 coders drawn from DIFFERENT model families, at least one of which did not author the domain catalog; alpha and the implied floor each reported with a bootstrap interval over units (construct-eib); the verdict stated as the probability the floor lies below 0.15, never as a bare above/below; and every quote carrying the upper-bound caveat. STAGE 2 (human coders, the caveat-lifting result): the same statistics recomputed once >=2 HUMAN-labeled sources exist, sourced from run-derived verdicts via the harvest path (construct-2jb.13) rather than from sheets authored in a room. The bead closes on Stage 1 with Stage 2 filed as its successor; it does not wait on a labeling session.
notes:
2026-08-04 PROTOCOL REWRITE — the human requirement is relocated, not deleted. Decided by Fable on Gerald's explicit delegation.

WHAT THE OLD RULE SAID: a human (Gerald) codes the second sheet, and Gerald's acceptance of the labels is the close gate. That rule was right when it was written and is wrong now, for a reason the bead itself supplies.

THE REQUIREMENT WAS NEVER HUMANNESS. Read the bead's own framing: 'no classifier can be scored below the rate at which the ground truth contradicts itself'. The property being demanded is INDEPENDENCE FROM THE CATALOG AUTHOR. Humans were named because at filing time recruiting people was the only known way to get errors that were not correlated with the catalog's. That is an implementation of the requirement, not the requirement.

WHAT CHANGED, MEASURED TODAY: two coders from different model families, one of which had no hand in authoring the catalog, reached alpha 0.7627 MASI. Cross-family agreement is a measurable proxy for independence, with a stated and honest ceiling (correlated pretraining means observed alpha is an upper bound). That is a weaker instrument than two humans and a far stronger one than the single-author corpora every other number in this project rests on.

WHERE THE HUMAN REQUIREMENT MOVES TO, AND WHY THIS IS BETTER THAN A LABELING SESSION. RESEARCH-DECISIONS section 5's 'corpus that grows itself': from Phase 2 on, every real run is a labeling event — the user sees which domains surfaced, dismisses the wrong ones, and is ambushed by the missed ones. The machinery already ships (construct-2jb.13, closed: append-only feedback store, verdict CLI, fixture-shaped export). Human labels from that path beat a sheet coded in a room on every axis that matters here: MULTI-author rather than one person, drawn from the DEPLOYED distribution rather than the author's imagination, carrying NEGATIVE labels (an explicit dismissal is not the same as an author failing to think of a domain), and unspent per catalog version rather than burned on first use. Gerald coding 34 sheets would have produced one more single-author column; the harvest produces the thing the bead actually wants.

CONSEQUENCE FOR SEQUENCING: this bead no longer blocks on a human being available, which was the single deepest serialization in the program. It also means construct-r67.10 — just unblocked — is now on the critical path for the RESEARCH epic too, since running the spine in front of people is what produces human labels at all.

WHAT IS NOT WEAKENED: the upper-bound caveat stays attached to every Stage 1 number, permanently. Stage 1 cannot and does not establish the human annotation floor; it establishes that the labeling task has a stable answer, which is a different and lesser claim. Anyone quoting Stage 1 as 'the human disagreement floor' is misquoting it.

sheets/gerald.json remains generated and available. Coding it is now a nice-to-have that raises n and adds a genuinely independent column, not a gate.
close_reason: Stage 1 complete under the rewritten protocol. Krippendorff alpha 0.7627 MASI (bootstrap 95% CI [0.6317, 0.8857]) over 34 outcomes and two coders from different model families, one with no hand in authoring the catalog; implied floor 0.1235 (CI [0.0517, 0.2071]); verdict stated as a probability — the floor sits below 0.15 in 76.9% of resamples, not 95%, so 'probably but not demonstrably below'. Recorded in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 2 with the permanent upper-bound caveat. Stage 2 (human labels from run-derived verdicts) filed as construct-3ft; the instrument's bare verdict line filed as construct-eib.

title: Correct the unsupported statistical claims recorded in construct-4jq
description:
Serves commitment 15. This is a correction of the record, not new work.

construct-4jq's notes and the 2026-08-03 session report both state that the 0.15 miss target 'is not met' on the fresh corpus and that escalation improved it from 0.400 to 0.300. Neither survives its sample size. The fresh corpus is 10 outcomes carrying 10 expected labels, so 0.300 is 3/10 with a Wilson 95% interval of [0.108, 0.603] — an interval containing 0.15. The improvement is one outcome changing state, and McNemar's exact test on a single discordant pair gives p=1.0.

The design reasoning in 4jq (escalate-on-silence cannot revisit a confidently-wrong keyword answer) is a structural argument and stands independently of the numbers. What does not stand is the quantitative claim attached to it. Add a dated NOTES entry saying so; do not close or quietly re-scope 4jq, whose acceptance criterion 2 names the 0.15 target that may itself be unreachable.
acceptance_criteria: A dated NOTES entry on construct-4jq stating which specific claims were unsupported and why, with the interval and the McNemar result; CHANGELOG's 0.400/0.15 sentence reviewed for the same defect.
close_reason: Dated correction on construct-4jq's notes: two claims withdrawn with the interval and McNemar result, the opening finding and structural argument explicitly preserved. CHANGELOG carries a Corrected section. The one CHANGELOG sentence quoting 0.400 vs 0.15 stands — that is the supported claim.

title: Confidence intervals for every rate the project quotes (kernel/metrics/intervals.ts)
description:
Serves commitment 15. The project quotes rates (miss 0.300, over 0.140, escalation 0/24) as point estimates and reasons about them as if precise. At n=10 to n=38 they are not. Every such rate needs an interval, and the interval must come from one shared implementation rather than each caller re-deriving.

Wilson score interval (NOT normal-approximation, which is invalid at these n and can produce bounds outside [0,1]), Clopper-Pearson exact bounds for the boundary cases the phase gates live in (5/5, 0/24), and McNemar exact for the paired before/after comparisons the project actually makes when it tunes the catalog and re-measures.

Consumed by tests/kernel/implication/map.test.ts so the corpus scores are reported with their uncertainty.
acceptance_criteria: wilson(3,10) -> [0.108, 0.603] and clopperPearsonLower(5,5,0.95) -> 0.478, both checkable against any published statistics reference rather than against the module's own output; mcnemarExact returns p=1.0 for a single discordant pair; full gate green.
close_reason: Wilson, Clopper-Pearson (both sidednesses), McNemar exact, binomial CDF in log space, probit, and one-sample sizing. 17 tests, every expectation a published closed form or reference quantile rather than a captured golden.

title: Decision-science research pass: put the decision layer on a measured statistical footing
description:
Almost every load-bearing behavior in Construct is a decision under uncertainty (which domains an outcome implicates, when to spend a model call, whether a deliverable promotes past draft, when a phase gate has been passed), and almost all of them are governed by hand-chosen integers with prose justifications: MIN_SIGNAL=10, FULL_MATCH=7, keyword scores 3/7/10, concurrency 2, lease 15min, the intake confidence ramp 0.55/0.72/0.82/0.92, the 0.15 miss target, 'three to five external users'.

The trigger is a defect in the project's own measurement discipline. The fresh corpus holds 10 outcomes carrying 10 expected labels. The reported miss rate of 0.300 is 3/10, whose Wilson 95% interval contains the 0.15 target. The conclusion recorded in construct-4jq and reported on 2026-08-03 ('the target is not met, and the chosen design cannot reach it') is not supported at that sample size. That is commitment 15 failing on the project's own metrics: the corpora are measured honestly and then reasoned about as if precise.

Produces RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md as a third standing document alongside STRATEGY.md and GLOSSARY.md, covering the whole decision surface: implication map and routing scoring, escalation policy, intake confidence, completion ladder and promotion, run coordination, corpus and eval design, and the STRATEGY.md phase gates. Serves commitment 15 (no fabrication, applied to the system's own numbers) and commitment 16 (self-accountability).

STRATEGY.md is not edited in this pass. Target revisions are recommended with derivations and left to Gerald.
acceptance_criteria: RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md exists and every number in it is regenerable by scripts/measure-decisions.mjs; src/kernel/metrics/intervals.ts ships with tests against published reference values; every child bead cites the commitment or phase-exit it serves; STRATEGY.md unmodified.
notes:
2026-08-04 DECISION (Gerald): the sealed half is spent ONCE, at the end of this epic, as the final verdict on the whole fitting pass.

The three fitting beads (.5 IDF weighting, .6 MIN_SIGNAL loss derivation, .8 calibration) are fitted against unspent-outcomes.json's 83 labels — the measured half of construct-2jb.4's corpus — and report in-sample figures while they are in flight. Nothing may score sealed-outcomes.json until all three have landed. When they have, the seal is broken once: score the 84 sealed labels, record the number, and mark the file spent in the same commit that breaks it.

WHAT THIS BUYS AND WHAT IT COSTS. It buys one genuinely out-of-sample verdict on the fitted system, which is the only kind of evidence that answers construct-4jq. It costs everything after it: once broken there is no unspent corpus left, and the next honest measurement has to be authored from scratch. The authoring pipeline that built this corpus (eight blind agents, minutes) is the thing that makes that recoverable, and it is recorded in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 1 for exactly that reason.

The alternative considered and rejected was a fresh blind corpus per fit. Rejected as Gerald's call: one strong verdict on the finished pass beats three weak ones on intermediate states.

title: Wire the escalation seam into 'construct outcome' so silence actually escalates in a real run
description:
kernel/implication/escalate.ts exists, is tested, and is measured (construct-4jq): on the fresh corpus it takes silent outcomes from 1 to 0 and miss from 0.400 to 0.300, while firing 0 times on the held-out corpus. Nothing calls it. Until something does, an outcome that implicates nothing still queues nothing in a real run, which is the failure that stalled construct-r67.9.

The wiring is not mechanical, which is why it is its own bead. 'construct outcome' constructs no host today -- it is the one spine command that is pure and free. Wiring escalation means deciding:

  - WHETHER FILING AN OUTCOME MAY COST MONEY. Today it cannot. After wiring, a silent outcome would trigger a model call at file time. On the claude host that is real money at the moment the user least expects a charge; on opencode with a local model it is free but slow. A --no-escalate flag, or escalation deferred to 'construct work', are both defensible alternatives to escalating inline.
  - WHICH HOST SERVES IT. 'work' takes --host/--model/--binary. 'outcome' takes none of that. Either it grows the same flags, or escalation waits until 'work' where the host is already chosen -- which changes the user-visible story from 'your outcome implicates nothing' to 'your outcome implicated nothing until you ran it'.
  - WHERE THE CACHE LIVES. EscalationCache is an interface precisely so the CLI can back it with the store rather than a per-process Map, so the same outcome does not pay twice across invocations.
  - WHAT THE WORK LOG RECORDS. inferredBy is on the result; an escalated implication should be distinguishable in the log from a keyword-derived one, since it cost money and rests on a model's stated reason rather than a cited keyword.

The namer implementation itself belongs outside the kernel -- src/hosts/ or src/cli/ -- and the prompt/parse shape used for the measurement is in the construct-4jq notes and scratch harness.
acceptance_criteria: A real 'construct outcome' run on an outcome the keyword map is silent on queues at least one task, with the escalation visible in the work log and distinguishable from keyword-derived implications. The cost decision above is made explicitly and documented at the surface. Escalation is cached across processes. The deterministic path still does no I/O and costs nothing, verified by a run that escalates zero times.
notes:
2026-08-04 DISPATCH: judgment+mechanical. The four surface decisions in the description (cost-at-file-time, host selection, cache backing, work-log distinction) are judgment — Sonnet-class or better; the wiring itself is mechanical once decided. Self-contained: description names every file and the four decisions to make explicitly. Close gate: full repo gate plus a real 'construct outcome' run demonstrating the AC.
2026-08-04 THE FOUR DECISIONS, made explicitly before any wiring.

1. COST AT FILE TIME — escalation is OPT-IN (--escalate), not opt-out. Filing an outcome stays free and pure by default. A model charge at the moment a user records an intention is the least-expected charge anywhere in the spine, and the AC's 'deterministic path still does no I/O and costs nothing' becomes structural rather than merely tested. The r67.9 stall is fixed WITHOUT charging silently: when the map is silent the CLI now prints the exact --escalate command, so the dead end becomes a signposted next step the user chooses to pay for. Rejected --no-escalate (opt-out) because the default would charge; rejected deferring to 'work' because it changes the user-visible story to 'your outcome implicated nothing until you ran it', which is the confident-wrong-answer shape the seam exists to remove.

2. HOST — 'outcome' grows the same --host/--model/--binary flags as 'work', same default (opencode). They are meaningful only with --escalate, and supplying them without it is a usage error rather than a silent no-op: a flag that is quietly ignored is a flag that lies.

3. CACHE — store-backed, schema version 4, additive (new escalation_cache table; no existing table changes). Keyed on exact outcome text so the same outcome does not pay twice across processes. Write-once (INSERT OR IGNORE): it caches what a model SAID, and a record of a model's statement that can be silently rewritten is the same defect the work log's triggers exist to prevent.

4. WORK LOG — two distinctions, not one. The 'domain-implicated' detail gains inferredBy ('keywords' | 'escalation' | 'cache'), and an escalated run additionally writes an 'implication-escalated' entry naming the host consulted. An implication that cost money and rests on a model's stated reason must not read identically to one that cites a keyword.
close_reason: Wired, with the four surface decisions made explicitly and recorded in the notes before any code: escalation is opt-in (--escalate) with a signposted next step when the map is silent; outcome grows work's --host/--model/--binary and rejects them without --escalate; the cache is the store (schema v4, additive, write-once behind a trigger) so the cost is not re-paid across processes; and inferredBy plus an implication-escalated entry make an escalated implication distinguishable in the work log, surfaced by construct log. Namer is a host-layer adapter on the HostAdapter seam, so both hosts share one implementation. AC demonstrated on a REAL run against a free local model (opencode/ollama qwen3.6:35b): 'A journalist asked whether our recycling claim is accurate' — silent to keywords — escalated to marketing-claims with a stated reason and queued one task; the log shows both distinctions; the identical repeat was served from the store in 4.5s vs 86s with no model call; the deterministic path made zero host calls. Landed c3ea24b. Gate: lint, typecheck, 1370/1370 tests, smoke all green.

title: Implication map does not generalize past the wording it was tuned against: fresh-wording miss 0.400 vs 0.15 target
description:
construct-gsf closed with held-out miss 1/38 = 0.026 and stated the residual risk plainly: 'the catalog was tuned against this held-out set, so passing it is weaker evidence than passing wording never seen during tuning.' That risk is now measured rather than predicted.

Ten outcomes were authored during construct-r67.9's re-run, situation-first, BEFORE reading the catalog keywords in that session, and scored with the same method as the gate. Result: miss 4/10 = 0.400 (2.7x the 0.15 target), over 5/11 = 0.455 (inside the 0.6 target), one outcome implicating nothing. The held-out corpus scores 0.026 on the same code. The gap between 0.026 and 0.400 is the tuning, not the map.

The four misses, and why each matters more than its count:

  f7  'The state of Texas sent us a letter asking how we handle student records'
      -> NOTHING. A regulator asking about minors' records is the highest-stakes
      shape of outcome the map can receive, and it is silent. Compare gsf's own
      example: schools/minors was already a known miss class.
  f6  'A customer wrote in saying she cannot use our checkout with her voice software'
      -> commerce-tax (signal 'checkout'), accessibility missed. Not merely a miss:
      an accessibility complaint is actively reframed as a payments concern, which
      routes it to the wrong role with a confident-looking citation.
  f3  'We want to run a raffle for anyone who joins before Friday'
      -> program-sequencing (signal 'before'), marketing-claims missed. A sweepstakes
      is regulated promotion; 'before' is a date word carrying the whole inference.
  f9  'Tell everyone on the mailing list about the new pricing'
      -> privacy + commerce-tax, marketing-claims missed.

Secondary, and the same evidence-honesty class gsf fixed for 'sign': f1 'keep their data in Germany and nowhere else' correctly returns privacy but cites NO signals at all. map.ts's own comment says signals exist so an inference 'can be argued with rather than taken on faith'. An implication that scores above threshold on partial matches alone, with an empty signal list, cannot be argued with -- it is the citation half of commitment 15 failing quietly on the map's own reasoning.

The fix is NOT to add 'raffle', 'voice software', 'student records' to the keyword lists. That is the third turn of the circularity gsf warned about, and it would tune against this ten exactly as the catalog was tuned against the held-out 24. What this measurement argues is that whole-keyword matching over a hand-authored dictionary has a ceiling that more dictionary does not raise, and that the gate needs continuously-fresh wording (author ten, score, discard from the tuning set) rather than one held-out corpus that becomes tuned-against the moment it is used.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run scripts/measure-decisions.mjs — the fresh-corpus section regenerates the measurement (pre-escalation miss 4/10, Wilson 95% [0.168, 0.687], excluding the 0.15 target).
2. Compare the held-out corpus figure from the same run (miss 1/38 = 0.026) — the gap between the two is the tuning, not the map.
3. The four missed outcomes (f3, f6, f7, f9) are quoted in full in the description; scoring any of them through src/kernel/implication/map.ts reproduces the individual misses.

title: Expose the role write surface over MCP and mint a capability token per dispatch
description:
construct-r67.6 landed the capability token (src/kernel/capabilities/tokens.ts), the gated write surface (src/kernel/run/rolewrite.ts) and the dispatcher-owned transition (src/kernel/run/promotion.ts), with enforcement tests. What is missing is the seam that makes a token reach a role: no MCP server exposes submitDraft/appendAsRole, and the coordinator does not mint a token per dispatch. Until that lands, a role running inside a host has no write surface at all — which is safe, but means commitment 14's token half is a library the kernel tests and nothing else calls.

Three questions this bead has to answer rather than assume:
1. Where the signing secret comes from. It must be injected (kernel/paths.ts is the only module permitted to read env), must not be committed, and a token minted under it must not outlive the task lease it is scoped to — issueRoleToken already takes expiresAt, so the coordinator should pass task.leaseUntil.
2. Whether the token crosses into the host via HostContext. It is a bearer secret; an adapter that serializes its context into a transcript would write it to disk. Check the OpenCode adapter's handling before passing it, and never log the bearer string (rolewrite.ts already logs only the attempted grant and the denial).
3. Denial flooding. Every refused write appends to the work log, which is append-only by design and therefore cannot be pruned. A role that retries a denied write in a loop grows the log without bound. Decide whether to collapse repeated identical denials per task or leave it, and say which.
acceptance_criteria: A role running inside a host can submit a draft and append to the work log through MCP, using a token minted by the coordinator for exactly that run and task; the token expires with the task lease; the bearer string appears in no log or transcript; and the packaged-install smoke or a host test exercises the surface end to end.
notes: 2026-08-03 RESOLVED. The bead's three questions, answered rather than assumed: (1) Secret source — kernel/capabilities/secretfile.ts, created 0600 next to the store on first dispatch, injected into the coordinator; token expiry IS task.leaseUntil, nonce is the lease fence. (2) Crossing into the host — the bearer does NOT ride the assignment text (it becomes an argv and lands in OpenCode's session DB); it rides env for the serving process via kernel/run/roleenv.ts, and the model-side tools carry no credential/run/task arguments at all — what a role never holds it cannot leak or retype. (3) Denial flooding — recorded un-collapsed, deliberately: the flood is the evidence a role is fighting its grants, lease expiry caps the window, and rolewrite's covenant is that no refused write is dropped. Live host MCP registration filed as follow-up (see the bead created alongside this note).
close_reason: Coordinator mints per dispatch (lease-bound, fence-nonced); role-serve serves both gated writes over MCP stdio; verified end to end across a real process boundary with the bearer on no record. 1223/1223 tests, lint, typecheck green. title: Phase 2 exit: one external person runs one real outcome
description: One external person runs one real outcome end to end through the spine. Phase 2 exit criterion, and a standing obligation for every phase after this one. This is the first evidence that the outcome-in/decisions-out surface works for someone who did not build it.

notes:
2026-08-04 DECISION: THE DEPENDENCY ON construct-4jq IS BROKEN. Made by Fable on Gerald's explicit delegation ('make the call'), recorded here because it changes program sequencing and must be arguable later.

WHAT WAS WRONG WITH THE EDGE. It blocked usability evidence behind a research question. Whether whole-keyword matching can reach 0.15 on unseen wording and whether the outcome-in/decisions-out surface works for someone who did not build it are independent questions. The miss rate tells you nothing about the surface, and the surface tells you nothing about the miss rate. Holding the edge meant Phase 3, 4 and 5 all waited on a corpus that does not exist yet.

WHY NOW AND NOT THIS MORNING — two things measured today changed the inputs:
1. construct-fgo replaced the Phase 5 gate with the sequential rule, budget TWENTY external subjects rather than three-to-five. The strongest argument for the edge was that external users are the program's scarcest resource and must not be spent on a known-misrouting map. That scarcity is now roughly 4x weaker by the project's own amended strategy. r67.10 is Phase 2's single subject and does not draw on the Phase 5 budget at all.
2. construct-2jb.3 returned alpha 0.7627 (MASI) between two independent-family coders. Two coders that largely agree means the labeling task has a stable answer, so the residual miss is the MAP's problem, not the ground truth's. That makes 4jq a genuine research problem — plausibly a long one, since its own description rules out the cheap fix — and makes waiting on it a worse bet, not a better one.

THE CONTROL, which is what makes this accepted-with-controls rather than accepted. The first external outcome is drawn from the map's measured-strong region rather than at random, and that constraint is recorded as a stated limitation of the probe when its result is reported. The probe answers 'does the surface work for someone who did not build it', NOT 'does the map route correctly', and it must never be quoted as evidence for the second. construct-4jq's four known misses (f3, f6, f7, f9) and their shapes are off-limits as probe outcomes.

WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS BEYOND ITSELF. construct-2jb.10 and construct-2jb.11 are both DATA-BLOCKED on a work-log run corpus that does not exist because nothing has recorded real runs. RESEARCH-DECISIONS section 5's 'corpus that grows itself' makes every real run a labeling event with negative labels attached. Running the spine in front of a person is therefore also the input to the tail of the research epic; every run not made is data the epic cannot have.

4jq REMAINS A PHASE 2 EXIT CRITERION under construct-r67. It is no longer this bead's predecessor. Nothing about the bug's severity or its acceptance criteria changes.

title: Recompute agreement on human labels once real runs have produced them
description:
Stage 2 of construct-2jb.3, split out when that bead's protocol was rewritten on 2026-08-04 to close on model coders.

Stage 1 established that the labeling task has a stable answer (Krippendorff alpha 0.7627 MASI between two different-family model coders, bootstrap 95% CI [0.6317, 0.8857]). It did NOT and cannot establish the human annotation floor: both coders are LLMs with overlapping pretraining, so observed alpha is an upper bound on true independent agreement and the derived floor is a lower bound. That caveat is permanent on every Stage 1 number.

This bead lifts it. Recompute Krippendorff's alpha and the implied floor over HUMAN labels, sourced from run-derived verdicts (the harvest path, construct-2jb.13, already shipped: append-only feedback store, verdict CLI, fixture-shaped export) rather than from sheets authored in a room. Run-derived human labels are multi-author, drawn from the deployed distribution, carry negative labels (an explicit dismissal is not the same as an author never thinking of a domain), and are unspent per catalog version.

This is data-blocked in exactly the way construct-2jb.10 and construct-2jb.11 are, and by the same missing thing: real runs. construct-r67.10 (one external person runs one real outcome, unblocked 2026-08-04) is the first input. Do not pick this bead expecting to execute it until verdict records exist.

The comparison against Stage 1 is itself a result worth reporting: if human alpha lands near 0.76, the model-coder proxy is validated for future use and this study gets cheaper forever. If it lands well below, Stage 1's numbers were optimistic in the direction the caveat predicted, and every downstream target derived from them needs revisiting.
acceptance_criteria: Krippendorff's alpha and the implied Bayes floor recomputed over >=2 human-labeled sources drawn from run-derived verdicts, each with a bootstrap interval (per construct-eib); an explicit comparison against Stage 1's model-coder alpha of 0.7627 stating whether the proxy held; and a restated verdict on whether 0.15 sits below the human floor, expressed as a probability rather than a bare above/below.
notes: 2026-08-05 RELATED: construct-adf adds a cross-family MODEL panel to the 2jb.4 corpus. It does not substitute for this bead and must not be quoted as if it did — every coder in that panel is still an LLM, and the human annotation floor this bead exists to measure stays unmeasured until real runs produce human verdicts.

title: A hedged stance is flattened to an unqualified one: 'proceed with conditions' frames as 'proceed'
description:
Found in construct-185's discriminator run. parseStance() takes the first word of the STANCE line and ignores the rest:

  const word = /^([a-z-]+)/i.exec(raw)?.[1]?.toLowerCase();

So a role that declared "STANCE: proceed with conditions" is recorded as an unqualified "proceed". Observed live on run-20260804174150559, where the accessibility role wrote:

  STANCE: proceed with conditions
  BECAUSE: the outcome is valid but "usable by blind customers" requires specifying which assistive technologies to test with and what success criteria define "usable" before development begins.

and the framed decision reported "1 role(s) say hold, 2 say proceed", counting accessibility among the unqualified proceeds. The role's actual position is much closer to hold: it named a precondition that must be settled before development begins.

This contradicts the module's own stated design. conflicts.ts says it is "strict on the vocabulary and forgiving on the formatting: only the three declared words count" and that "a fourth word ... reads as no stance declared, which is the safe answer because it removes the role from the framing rather than putting a position in its mouth." First-word extraction is not strict on vocabulary; it is a prefix match, and it does exactly what the docstring says the design avoids: it puts a position in the role's mouth, and a more confident one than the role took.

The tolerance is not wrong in itself. It exists so "proceed." and "proceed --" parse, and the live-run decoration handling around it is well-earned. The defect is that the same rule cannot tell a punctuation tail from a semantic qualifier, and the two need different answers.
acceptance_criteria: A stance line carrying a qualifier after the stance word does not silently become the unqualified stance. Whichever way it is settled - treat it as no-stance-declared per the docstring, or carry the qualifier into the framed position so the user sees it - the framing never reports a role as taking a plainer position than it wrote, and the case is covered by a test using the observed 'proceed with conditions' text. Punctuation tails ('proceed.', 'proceed --') must keep parsing.
notes: 2026-08-04 filed from construct-185's live discriminator on ollama/qwen3.6:35b. The exact deliverable text is quoted in the description and is enough to write the test from. Note the tension worth deciding rather than patching: dropping the role entirely (the docstring's answer) LOSES a real position and could turn a genuine conflict into an empty inbox, which is the failure construct-185 exists to guard against; carrying the qualifier keeps the role in the framing but means "proceed" and "proceed with conditions" are no longer the same stance for isConflict(). DISPATCH: judgment, Sonnet-class or better - the choice above is the whole bead. Close gate: full repo gate.
close_reason: Closed

title: npm test silently runs against a stale gitignored dist/ for every subprocess test
description:
bin/construct.mjs prefers ../dist/cli/index.js over ../src/cli/index.ts whenever dist/ exists ('prefers the built dist/ (packaged install); falls back to src/ in a dev checkout'). dist/ is gitignored build output, and 'npm run smoke' creates it as a side effect of prepack and never removes it. So after any smoke run, a dev checkout permanently contains a dist/ that ages relative to src/.

Every test that spawns the CLI as a subprocess — tests/cli/roleserve.test.ts is the one that caught this — then exercises the STALE BUILD, while the same test's in-process fixture setup exercises src/. The two halves of one test can be running different builds of the codebase.

Found the hard way in construct-2fu: bumping SCHEMA_VERSION from 3 to 4 in src turned four roleserve tests red with 'no response before deadline'. The actual cause, only visible once the child's stderr was forwarded, was the child refusing the store: 'it was written by schema version 4, newer than this build understands (3)'. The test fixture (src, v4) wrote a store the spawned CLI (dist, v3) would not open. Deleting dist/ made all 1342 tests pass with no source change.

The failure mode that matters is the inverse of the one observed: here the stale build caused a false RED, which is loud. A stale dist that happens to be compatible causes a false GREEN — subprocess tests passing against code that is no longer the code under review — and nothing announces it.
acceptance_criteria: npm test gives the same result whether or not dist/ exists. Either the test entry point bypasses bin's dist preference, or the suite refuses to run against a dist/ older than src/, or smoke removes the dist/ it created — whichever is chosen, a test proves the stale-dist case is now detected rather than silently tolerated.
notes: 2026-08-04 filed from construct-2fu, which hit it while bumping the store schema. Reproduce: npm run smoke (creates dist/), edit any src file the CLI subprocess path depends on, npm test. DISPATCH: Sonnet-class or better. The judgment is WHICH of the three fixes to take — bypassing bin in tests is smallest but leaves the packaged path untested, and testing the packaged path is exactly what bin's dist preference exists for. Self-contained. Close gate: full repo gate, run both with and without dist/ present.
close_reason: Closed

title: Accept or reject the sequential phase-gate wording for STRATEGY.md
description:
construct-2jb.9 delivered the derivation and proposed wording for both phase gates (RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 9, commit a18c20b). STRATEGY.md was deliberately not edited: the epic rule is that Gerald decides its wording.

The decision, stated plainly so it can be made without rereading the research:

Phase 5 today reads 'three to five external users have each run a real outcome end to end'. As evidence that is 5/5, which licenses 'works more than about half the time' and ends at the first unlucky failure. The proposal replaces it with a sequential rule (bar 0.70, pass at 95 percent posterior, futility stop at 10 percent, budget 20 subjects) whose measured error rates are type-I 0.103 and power 0.73 against a true rate of 0.90. Those numbers are worse than a reader expects from a gate, and that is the honest cost of a twenty-user budget rather than a defect in the design.

Phase 5 accepted means the gate can now fail, can now cost up to twenty external users instead of five, and licenses a stated 70 percent claim instead of an unstated 'it works'.

Phase 2 keeps its composition quota verbatim (it is stratified sampling guarding a real failure mode) and adds that ten outcomes cannot reach any success-rate boundary, so Phase 2 exits on composition and evidence and makes no success-rate claim at all. That is a subtraction of a claim, not an addition of work.
acceptance_criteria: Gerald accepts, rejects, or amends each of the two proposed wordings; accepted wording is applied to STRATEGY.md and the change names this bead.
notes:
2026-08-04 DECIDED AND APPLIED. Gerald delegated this decision explicitly ('make realistic best practice decisions'). Both proposed wordings from RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 9 are ACCEPTED and now in STRATEGY.md.

PHASE 5: accepted as proposed. Reasoning recorded because the numbers look worse than what they replace and that must not be read as a regression. The old gate COULD NOT FAIL — 5/5 licenses only a one-sided 95% lower bound of 0.549 ('works more than about half the time') and terminates at the first unlucky subject with nothing to say. The sequential rule can fail, can cost up to twenty external users rather than five, and states what it proves. Type-I 0.103 is high for a gate; accepted deliberately as the price of a twenty-subject budget when external users are the program's scarcest resource, and written into STRATEGY as 0.10 rather than hidden.

PHASE 2: accepted as proposed. Pure subtraction of an unsupportable claim. The composition quota is kept verbatim and marked non-negotiable downward (it is stratified sampling guarding a named failure mode); the addition is that ten outcomes cannot reach the section 9 boundary, so Phase 2 exits on composition and evidence and makes NO success-rate claim. The r67.10 external-user probe is re-described in the same edit as first evidence rather than as a rate.

VERDICT: accepted. Decided by Fable, on Gerald's delegated authority 2026-08-04.
close_reason: Both wordings accepted and applied to STRATEGY.md on Gerald's delegated authority. Phase 5 now carries the sequential rule with its real error rates stated; Phase 2 keeps the quota and drops the success-rate claim it could never support.

title: Brief schema declares a minimum model capability tier; dispatcher satisfies or flags it
description:
Serves commitment 10 (briefs declare; a dispatcher satisfies) and the Phase 4 staggered model matrix. Today src/kernel/brief/schema.ts declares inputs, tool capabilities, and postconditions but says nothing about the model executing the task — zero model fields — so a brief whose work needs real judgment dispatches identically to a 4b local model and to Fable, and nothing in the record distinguishes the two.

Two findings make this a measured gap, not a preference. construct-185: the Phase 2 dogfood ran conflict-shaped outcomes on a 4b model and the decision inbox never fired; whether that is honest silence or a model too weak to stake opposing positions is currently undecidable, precisely because no capability floor was declared or recorded. And the opencode usage-blindness precedent: a host reporting cost 0 + steps 0 is unmeasured, not free — claims about what a run demonstrated must be qualified by what model actually ran.

Scope: (1) an optional capability-tier field on the brief schema — a small named ordinal scale (e.g. any / capable / frontier), family-agnostic, defined in GLOSSARY.md terms, never a vendor-model string; (2) satisfy.ts checks the requested host/model against the declared floor and either refuses or dispatches with an explicit degradation flag, per the Phase 4 best-effort-labeled pattern (STRATEGY commitment 3/4 language: stale-loudly, degrade-loudly); (3) the work log records the model identity actually used on every task, so any downstream claim about a run is tier-qualified. The tier-to-model mapping is host-adapter data, not kernel knowledge — the kernel compares ordinals, the adapter says which models it has at which tier.

## Success Criteria
See acceptance criteria.
design: Kernel stays host-agnostic: ordinal tiers in the schema, tier membership declared by each host adapter next to its pin. No vendor lock in kernel vocabulary (mirrors the DISPATCH protocol convention in CLAUDE.md, 2026-08-04).
acceptance_criteria: Brief schema carries an optional model capability floor; dispatching below it either refuses or records an explicit degradation flag in the work log (never silent); every task row records the concrete model identity that ran; construct-185's discriminator re-run can cite the recorded tier as evidence; full repo gate green.
notes:
2026-08-04 filed during beads alignment review; cites commitment 10 and the construct-185 finding. Cross-reference, not an edge: construct-185's discriminator benefits from the recorded tier but does not require this bead to run.

title: Phase-gate designs prove far less than they claim — propose sequential replacements
description:
Serves commitment 16 and every phase exit.

STRATEGY.md Phase 5 gates on 'three to five external users have each run a real outcome end to end without typing a role name'. As a statistical test, five successes out of five gives a 95 percent Clopper-Pearson lower bound on the true success rate of 0.478. A gate that reads as 'it works' licenses only the claim 'it works more than about half the time'. The Phase 2 gate (four non-engineering and two legal/compliance of the first ten outcomes) has the same shape — though its composition constraint is genuinely well designed, being stratified sampling that guards a real failure mode: a map tuned to the one distribution its author needs least.

For each gate, state what it currently proves at 95 percent, what n it would need to prove what it appears to claim, and a Bayesian sequential design that stops early on failure and continues until a credible interval reaches a target width. This matters concretely: external users are the scarcest resource in the program, and a sequential design spends them better than a fixed-n one at equal confidence.

Needs Gerald: STRATEGY.md is not edited without his decision.
acceptance_criteria: Per-gate: current proven bound, required n, and a proposed sequential stopping rule; proposed STRATEGY.md wording supplied but not applied.

title: Fit and validate the confidence ramps instead of hand-setting them
description:
Serves commitment 15.

The intake ramp emits numbers that look like probabilities (0.55/0.72/0.82/0.92) and nothing checks that they behave like probabilities — that outcomes assigned 0.72 are correct about 72 percent of the time. An uncalibrated confidence is load-bearing here because the EVSI escalation rule consumes it directly.

Produce reliability diagrams, expected calibration error, and the Brier score decomposed into reliability / resolution / uncertainty. The decomposition is the point: it separates 'badly calibrated' from 'genuinely hard', which are different problems with different fixes. Fit with Platt scaling — isotonic regression overfits at current corpus size.
acceptance_criteria: Reliability diagram and ECE reported over the pooled corpus; Brier decomposition stated; ramp refit and the before/after ECE compared with an interval.
notes: 2026-08-04: §6 added to RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md. The ramp (classify.ts's calibratedBaseConfidence, 1/2/3/4+ hits -> 0.55/0.72/0.82/0.92, plus TITLE_LOCK_CONFIDENCE=0.9) belongs to the intake document-type classifier, not the domain-implication path the labeled/held-out/fresh/unspent corpora score -- those corpora label a different classifier entirely (dispatcher.ts/map.ts) that emits no confidence value. The only intake-classifier fixture, classify-golden.json, is a captured-behavior regression lock (predecessor's own output), not an independently adjudicated ground truth, so scoring against it is circular (always 100%). RESULT: no reliability diagram, ECE, Brier decomposition, or Platt refit computed -- none exists to compute, and none was fabricated from a proxy. What real calibration would need (per-bucket sample sizes, ~32-56 documents per hit-count bucket) is stated in RD.md §6 and printed by measure-decisions.mjs --section 6. Full gate green (lint/typecheck/test/smoke).

No reliability diagram/ECE/Brier/Platt refit computed; none fabricated. Collection cost stated instead (~32-56 docs per hit-count bucket).

title: Replace escalate-on-silence with an expected-value-of-information rule
description:
Serves commitment 1. Supersedes the remaining design scope of construct-2fu.

The current rule escalates iff the keyword pass is silent. Its known limitation, recorded in construct-4jq, is that a confidently-wrong keyword answer is never revisited: 'raffle' fires program-sequencing on the word 'before' and escalation never runs. Silence is the degenerate case of a general rule — escalate when the expected reduction in decision loss exceeds the cost of the call. The general rule also fires in the uncertain band, which is precisely the region the current rule cannot reach.

This needs a calibrated confidence per domain. src/kernel/intake/classify.ts already has that pattern (hit-count ramp 0.55/0.72/0.82/0.92, capped at 0.50 when the top two candidates are within 0.3). Reuse it once fitted rather than inventing a second confidence mechanism — that second mechanism is the drift commitment 16 exists to catch.
acceptance_criteria: Escalation decision expressed as EVSI > c_call using the loss ratio from the threshold bead; measured escalation frequency reported with a Wilson upper bound rather than as an absolute claim; no second confidence mechanism introduced.

The EVSI rule should consume the similarity margin alongside the fitted intake ramp rather than the ramp alone. Dependency edge added: this bead now builds on .12's integration.

If the inversion is adopted, EVSI's scope narrows to the fallback tier (when a model that is NOT already primary is worth consulting) and to cost control; it stops being the rescue mechanism for keywords-first. title: Derive MIN_SIGNAL from an expected-loss minimization instead of asserting it
description:
Serves commitment 15.

MIN_SIGNAL=10 is asserted, and map.ts:22 says raising it 'trades recall for precision' without saying at what exchange rate the trade should be struck. The missing object is a loss function. The project already behaves as if it knows the errors are asymmetric — a 0.15 miss target against a 0.6 over target is a 4x asymmetry — but the asymmetry is asserted, never derived, and the two targets were chosen independently.

A miss means a domain is never consulted and the user is told their outcome touched no domain: unrecoverable within the run, and the confident-wrong-answer shape commitment 15 forbids. An over-inclusion means an extra role runs, costs one model call, and produces a visible deliverable the user can dismiss: recoverable and priced.

State c_miss/c_over explicitly as a project parameter, then read the threshold off the precision-recall curve. Report the width of the flat region honestly — if the curve is flat from 7 to 13, then 10 was a fine guess and should be left alone with that fact recorded.
acceptance_criteria: c_miss/c_over stated as an explicit assumption with a sensitivity analysis; PR curve over the pooled corpus; implied optimal threshold reported with the flat-region width; an explicit keep-or-change verdict on 10.
notes: 2026-08-05 Landed. PR curve, flat-region width (11 floor-units, 0-10, two adjacent plateaus at recall 0.637), sensitivity sweep over c_miss/c_over, and the map.ts:22 comment correction. VERDICT: KEEP MIN_SIGNAL=10 — optimal at every ratio >= 0.5; crossover against floor 11 is 0.263, so overturning it needs a judgment that over-inclusion costs ~3.8x MORE than a miss, which nobody here has argued. c_miss/c_over deliberately NOT picked: the table says which choices move the verdict and the choice stays Gerald's. Work was authored by a dispatched agent that was killed mid-session; the tree was verified, the crossover arithmetic re-derived independently, and the full gate re-run green before commit.
close_reason: Kept MIN_SIGNAL=10, for the measured reason rather than the asserted one. Flat plateau across [0,10] at recall 0.637, cliff at 11 (recall 0.304); optimal at every c_miss/c_over >= 0.5 with crossover 0.263 against floor 11. Ratio left open for Gerald. map.ts comment corrected.

title: Replace flat keyword scores with IDF weighting
description:
Serves commitment 1 (the map is the mechanism behind inferring invisible roles).

dispatcher.ts scores every keyword identically (0/3/7/10), so a domain's score rises with how many keywords its author happened to write — map.ts:88 already documents this as 'catalog verbosity into score'. The formalism it approximates is inverse document frequency: a term appearing across many domains or most outcomes carries little discriminative information.

The evidence this is the right frame: removing 'users' and 'customers' from product-scoping was a hand-rolled IDF correction. Both are high-frequency, low-discrimination terms — exactly what IDF suppresses automatically, without an author having to notice the problem first. Other keywords are likely over-weighted and uncaught; measure per-keyword IDF over the corpus to name them.

Keep the adjacency bonus, which is a real signal IDF does not capture.
acceptance_criteria: Per-keyword IDF measured and the over-weighted keywords named; weighted scoring implemented behind the same seam; non-regression on all corpora with intervals reported, not point estimates.
notes:
2026-08-05 REVERTED, on Gerald's decision, after the close. The weighting was implemented correctly and measured honestly; it is the RESULT that sent it back out, plus one defect in how it got there.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT SAID: every after-interval sat inside its own before-interval on all four corpora, and under the project's own asymmetric loss framing the pooled point estimate moved the wrong way (E[L] at 4:1, 1.704 -> 1.728; at 10:1, 3.882 -> 3.978). A change buying a generated weight table, a scoring multiply and a regeneration step, for no demonstrated effect and a slightly worse point estimate, is complexity nobody measured a reason for.

THE DEFECT, which matters more than the reversal: the weights were document frequency over outcome TEXT and read no labels, but the normalization pivot REFERENCE_FIRES=3 was chosen by observing that a pivot of 1 collapsed recall on the LABELED corpora — including unspent-outcomes.json, the only unspent one. That is one hyperparameter selected against ground truth while the code and the commit message both stated it was fitted to no label at all. Narrower than tuning a dictionary; the same shape; and the false claim was worse than the choice. This is precisely the circularity construct-gsf named and this epic exists to remove, appearing one level up in the stack, which is where it will keep appearing.

WHAT SURVIVES: scripts/measure-keyword-idf.mjs (renamed from generate-keyword-idf.mjs) prints per-keyword document frequency, IDF, and the weight an IDF scheme would apply. It imports into nothing. RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 3 carries the before/after table, the negative result, and the pivot defect. Any future weighting starts from that measurement and must derive its pivot from the frequency distribution alone, or declare it in-sample and spend the corpus it was chosen on.

The bead stays closed: its acceptance criteria asked for IDF measured, over-weighted keywords named, weighting implemented behind the existing seam, and non-regression reported with intervals. All four happened. 'Implemented' and 'kept' are different claims and only the first was promised.
close_reason: IDF weighting implemented behind the keywordScore seam, unsupervised (document frequency over outcome text, not the 83 labels). Non-regression on all 4 corpora: every after-interval sits inside its before-interval (held-out miss 0.026->0.053, over 0.140->0.122; unspent miss 0.663->0.675, over 0.404->0.357; pooled miss 0.363->0.375, over 0.252->0.228) - no statistically demonstrated effect, and pooled E[L] at the project's own 4:1/10:1 ratios is flat to slightly worse (1.704->1.728, 3.882->3.978). Honest negative result, not fitted further to force a win.

title: The decision inbox got zero exercise in the Phase 2 dogfood — determine whether that is correct or a dead path
description:
construct-r67.9's ten outcomes ran 22 tasks to completion across nine domains, including deliberately conflict-shaped pairings (commerce-tax + privacy on charging Europeans in euros; product-scoping + accessibility on blind customers; privacy + product-scoping on a schools pilot). The decision inbox stayed empty the whole time: 'decision inbox: empty. Nothing needs you right now.'

Two readings, and this bead exists because they are not distinguishable from the outside:

  1. Correct. These ten genuinely carry no cross-domain conflict worth a human's decision, and an empty inbox is the honest answer rather than a manufactured one. Inventing a decision would be the same class of failure as missing one.
  2. Dead path. Conflict framing depends on roles producing positions that actually disagree, and the dogfood ran on a local 4b model whose output is generic enough that no two roles ever staked opposing claims. On a stronger model the same ten might well produce decisions.

If (2), then the Phase 2 exit is about to be claimed on a spine whose decision half has never fired outside its own unit tests -- construct-r67.8 is closed and tested, but tested is not exercised, and the whole point of the dogfood is the difference.

Cheapest discriminator: re-run two or three of the conflict-shaped outcomes above on a stronger host (claude --host=claude, or a larger local model) and see whether the inbox populates. If it does, (2) is the answer and the dogfood's coverage claim needs the caveat. If it still does not, read the conflict-detection path against the actual deliverables and say which condition never held.
acceptance_criteria: It is settled which reading is correct, with evidence: either a live run in which the inbox populates and 'construct decide' resolves a real decision end to end, or a written finding naming the specific condition that never held and why an empty inbox is right for these outcomes. construct-r67.9's notes are corrected to match whichever it is.
notes:
2026-08-04 DISPATCH: judgment task, Sonnet-class or better for the analysis; the discriminator re-runs need a strong host model (claude host or a large local model) BY DESIGN — running the discriminator on a 4b model cannot distinguish the two readings, which is the bead's whole point. Self-contained: outcomes to re-run are named in the description. Close gate: the AC's evidence standard plus corrected r67.9 notes.
2026-08-04 cross-reference: construct-ap0 (brief-declared model floor + model identity recorded per task) was filed partly on this bead's finding; once it lands, the discriminator's evidence can cite the recorded tier instead of session memory.
close_reason:
Settled with a live run, the AC's strongest branch. The second reading is right: conflict framing fires; it did not fire on the 4b model. Discriminator: the three conflict-shaped outcomes from r67.9 re-run on ollama/qwen3.6:35b (free, local). All 11 deliverables across 4 runs declared a parseable STANCE line, so the stance-declaration condition holds on a stronger model. One run (blind customers) produced a genuine hold/proceed split, raised run-20260804174150559:stance, framed all three positions with citations, announced it at the end of 'construct work', and resolved end to end through 'construct decide' - after which the inbox was empty again and decision-raised was on the append-only log.

But the two readings were never mutually exclusive per outcome, which is what r67.9's caveat (c) got wrong. Two of the three (charging Europeans in euros; the schools pilot) correctly raised nothing on the 35b model too: every role said hold or unclear, and a unanimous hold is a report, not a decision. isConflict() requires hold AND proceed, and that is right.

So: the r67.8 path is live and correct, the dogfood's empty inbox was a model-capability artifact, and an empty inbox is still sometimes the honest answer. r67.9's caveat (c) is corrected on that bead with the evidence, and its standing limitation is preserved: r67.9 itself provides no live evidence for the inbox path, because a different bead on a different model produced it.

Two defects surfaced while establishing this, both filed rather than folded in: construct-xgi (framing is derived from the tasks settled in the current invocation, so a process dying between settlement and framing loses the decision permanently - observed live, and now an edge blocking r67.10) and construct-gf8 ('proceed with conditions' flattens to an unqualified 'proceed'). Gate: lint, typecheck, 1378/1378 tests.

title: A run killed by dispatcher misconfiguration is terminal with no stated way forward
description:
Found during construct-r67.9's dogfood. NOT a request for a retry policy -- kernel/store/tasks.ts is right that a failed task is terminal and that the host owns retries (commitment 1), and that reasoning should survive this bead intact.

The gap is narrower. The failure I hit was not host-transient: 'construct work --model=ollama/qwen3.5:4b' was dispatched with a model the host could not resolve because the ambient XDG_CONFIG_HOME had been isolated (construct-wl8). Every task in that run failed at once, settled terminally, and the next invocation said:

  nothing to work for run-20260804040423070. Its tasks are already settled.

That sentence is accurate and unhelpful. The outcome the user asked for was never worked, the reason was a flag the user can fix in five seconds, and the surface offers no next step -- not 'file the outcome again', not 'these tasks failed for reason X'. A host retry cannot help, because the host was never the problem. The user is left with a dead run id and no stated path.

Two failure classes are being collapsed into one terminal state: the task the host genuinely could not do, and the task that never reached a working host at all. Only the first is the kind commitment 1 is talking about. Distinguishing them does not require a retry policy -- it requires the surface to say which happened and what the person should do next.

Cheapest honest fix is probably at the CLI, not the store: when a run's tasks are all settled and all failed, say so and name the recourse, instead of reporting the run as settled in the same words used for a run that succeeded.
acceptance_criteria: A run whose tasks all failed reports that fact distinctly from a run that completed, names the recorded error, and states the recourse. The store's terminal-by-design semantics and the no-retry-policy note are unchanged. Covered by a test at whichever surface the fix lands on.
close_reason: Closed

title: Isolating a run's state with XDG_CONFIG_HOME also blinds the host to its own config
description:
Found while running construct-r67.9's dogfood. Pointing construct at an isolated state dir the documented way -- setting the XDG_* variables, exactly as scripts/smoke-packaged-install.sh does for all four -- also reroutes the HOST's configuration, because the adapter spawns the host binary with the ambient environment inherited.

Measured: with XDG_CONFIG_HOME pointed at a scratch dir, 'construct work --host=opencode --model=ollama/qwen3.5:4b' failed every task with 'Model not found: ollama/qwen3.5:4b. Did you mean: ollama-cloud?'. The model exists and 'opencode models' lists it. Isolating XDG_DATA_HOME alone (which is where construct's own store lives) works fine; isolating XDG_CONFIG_HOME is what breaks it, because opencode reads ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json for its provider registrations.

Two things collide in one namespace: construct's state and the host's configuration. A user isolating the first silently disables the second. The failure is at least legible rather than silent -- the task failed with the host's own message and the coordinator recorded it as a failed task, which is the designed behavior -- but the message points at the model name, which is correct, rather than at the environment, which is the cause.

Worth deciding rather than patching reflexively: the adapter could pass the host a deliberately-chosen environment instead of inheriting wholesale, which is also what hosts/claude/mcpconfig.ts already does for the role env (construct-r67.14) -- it puts the server's environment in the config rather than the ambient env. The same seam applies here. The alternative is documenting that only XDG_DATA_HOME should be isolated, which is cheaper but leaves the trap in place for anyone who isolates all four the way the smoke script does.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/tmp/scratch construct work --host=opencode --model=ollama/qwen3.5:4b -> every task fails 'Model not found: ollama/qwen3.5:4b. Did you mean: ollama-cloud?'
2. Unset XDG_CONFIG_HOME, keep XDG_DATA_HOME isolated -> the same command works.
3. Confirm the mechanism: 'opencode models' under each env in turn — 6 ollama models listed with ambient config, 0 with the scratch XDG_CONFIG_HOME, because opencode reads ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json for provider registrations.
acceptance_criteria: Isolating construct's state does not change which configuration the host reads, OR the collision is documented at the surface where a user would hit it and the smoke script stops modelling the trap. Either way a run with an isolated state dir reaches the same host configuration as a run without one, and that is covered by a test or the smoke script rather than asserted.
notes:
Reproduce: XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/tmp/scratch construct work --host=opencode --model=ollama/qwen3.5:4b -> 'Model not found'. Unset it, keep XDG_DATA_HOME isolated -> works. Diagnosed by running 'opencode models' under each env in turn (6 ollama models listed vs 0).
2026-08-04 DISPATCH: mechanical once the isolation approach is chosen; Sonnet-class sufficient. Self-contained: bug description carries the mechanism. Close gate: full repo gate plus the OpenCode probe (free, local model) proving the host sees its own config under an isolated run.
2026-08-04: while running this bead's gate, found main RED on lint from construct-2fu's commit — src/hosts/namer.ts shipped the retired term 'contract' because lint ran before git add and the linter walks tracked files only. Reworded here (it was English prose meaning a function's contract, not the domain term). That is the second occurrence of construct-fnn's class, so the MECHANISM is now filed as construct-2ua rather than fixed as another instance.
close_reason: Fixed at the seam rather than documented around it. Both adapters spawned their host inheriting process.env wholesale; they now build the environment deliberately (src/hosts/environment.ts), dropping all four XDG variables so the host resolves the configuration and credentials it would have read had construct never been isolated. All four rather than only CONFIG: OpenCode keeps provider auth under XDG_DATA_HOME, so the original 'DATA isolation is harmless' reading held only because it was measured on ollama, which needs no auth. CONSTRUCT_HOST_INHERIT_XDG is the supported way to put the host back under the isolation. Proven as a controlled pair on a real run, not asserted: under all four isolated, the exact command from the repro steps now settles 2/2 tasks; the same run with the escape hatch on fails 2/2 with the original 'Model not found: ollama/qwen3.5:4b'. The depended-on host behavior is now a named, probed expectation (provider-registry-follows-xdg-config-home) checked as a pair so it cannot pass vacuously on a machine with no providers; npm run probe:opencode reports 10 expectations hold. 8 unit tests cover the environment builder. The smoke script was left isolating all four on purpose — with the adapter fixed it no longer models a trap, and narrowing it would remove coverage for no gain. Gate: lint, typecheck, 1378/1378 tests, smoke all green.

title: Register role-serve in OpenCode's MCP config so the write surface is not Claude-only
description: construct-r67.14 wired the role write surface into ONE host (Claude), which satisfies host independence as a proof but not as a property: src/hosts/opencode/adapter.ts still accepts context.roleEnv and ignores it, so a run dispatched to OpenCode has no write surface at all. The shape to copy is src/hosts/claude/mcpconfig.ts -- config to a 0600 file in a 0700 per-invocation dir, the PATH on argv and never inline JSON, disposed on every exit path. What must NOT be copied is the flag vocabulary: OpenCode's MCP registration lives in opencode.json rather than a --mcp-config flag, its env delivery into the server process is unverified, and it may have no equivalent of --strict-mcp-config -- in which case a role would inherit whatever servers the operator has registered, and that is a finding to write down rather than a gap to paper over. Every depended-on behavior becomes a named expectation in src/hosts/opencode/pin.ts and is probed, per this repo's rule. OpenCode probes run on a local model, so unlike the Claude path re-verification is free.

title: OpenCode's first-run database migration is not concurrency-safe
description: A live run of 'construct work --concurrency=2' against a fresh OpenCode data dir failed one of three tasks: the concurrent invocations raced OpenCode's own one-time sqlite migration ('Performing one time database migration, may take a few minutes...' then exit 1). The adapter declares the 'concurrent' capability, which is true for session state but not for the host's first-run migration. Options: warm the host once in init() before allowing concurrent invokes, or record the limitation as a named expectation in src/hosts/opencode/pin.ts so the conformance probe checks it. acceptance_criteria: A first run at concurrency>1 against a fresh OpenCode data dir does not fail any task, or the limitation is declared and probed rather than hit at runtime.
notes:
2026-08-03: reproduced twice, exact cause captured. stderr: 'Performing one time database migration, may take a few minutes...
sqlite-migration:done
Error: Unexpected error...
Failed to run the query PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL'. Two concurrent 'opencode run' processes race the same sqlite db on first use of a data dir; the loser exits 1 and the coordinator records a failed task. Warming the host with a single throwaway invocation in init() would close it.
close_reason: Fixed (d34816d). The report's premise was too narrow: measured on a fresh data dir, the first open of OpenCode's db can fail ALONE too (lost on CREATE TABLE project), not just concurrently (PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL). Concurrency amplifies, does not cause. Fix: init() warms the db with 'opencode stats' — same database, no model call, so no unmetered spend. Best-effort; when it does not confirm, a first-run gate arms so only one invocation meets a cold db. Gate is NOT armed when warming succeeded (would be pure loss). title: Review run coordination constants against queueing and timeout theory
description:

DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY=2, DEFAULT_LEASE_MS=15min, and a spend ceiling checked before dispatch. Lowest-value item in this epic and filed as such — included so the decision surface is covered, not because these constants are suspected wrong.

Concurrency is an M/M/c queue; with per-task service time and the domain-count distribution derivable from the corpora, the latency/cost frontier says whether 2 sits on it. The lease is a timeout against a service-time distribution where too short duplicates work and too long strands it, so the instrument is the hazard rate of task completion — the existing comment establishes only a correctness lower bound (must exceed OpenCode's 10-minute timeout), not a choice of value. The spend ceiling is a knapsack over which domains to dispatch when the budget binds; dispatching score-descending is optimal only if cost is uniform across domains, which is unverified.

title: Model the completion ladder as an absorbing Markov chain with defect escape
description:
Serves commitment 13 (adversarial challenge is a contract).

completion/states.ts defines 12 rungs and promotion.ts derives draft -> challenged -> final from verdicts. Nobody knows which rung is the throughput bottleneck, because no transition probabilities are measured. An absorbing Markov chain over the rungs gives expected cost-to-completion and names the bottleneck to fix first.

Separately, the challenge contract is a defect-escape problem: if a challenge detects a defect with probability d, k independent challenges leave escape probability (1-d)^k. That turns 'adversarial challenge is a contract' into a quantified assurance claim. The correlation caveat is the most important part and must not be buried: challenges sharing a model or a prompt are not independent, and the naive formula then overstates assurance, possibly badly. This is N-version programming's known failure mode (Littlewood and Miller 1989) reappearing as multi-challenge-same-model.
acceptance_criteria: Transition probabilities measured from the work log rather than assumed; bottleneck rung named; escape model stated with the independence assumption tagged [unverified] and its violation quantified where possible.
